Transcript: Here's a question that sounds simple: what does a typical planetary system look like? For most of history we had exactly one example, our own, so we couldn't really answer it. Then in 1995 astronomers found a planet circling an ordinary Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi, and it was bizarre. It had roughly half the mass of Jupiter, and it went around its star in about four days. Four days! Mercury takes eighty-eight. A giant planet that close to its star had no place in the theories of the time.

Over the next few years, more of these so-called hot Jupiters turned up, one after another. So you might conclude that this is what planetary systems usually look like, and that ours is the odd one out. And for a while, a lot of people did conclude that.

Here's the catch. Think about how those planets were found. The main technique watched for a star wobbling back and forth as a planet tugged on it. Now, which planets tug hardest and fastest? Massive ones in tight orbits. A hot Jupiter makes a big wobble that repeats every few days, so you can confirm it in a single observing season. A planet like our Jupiter takes about twelve years to complete one orbit, and its wobble is far smaller. The method wasn't sampling planets. It was sampling the planets that were easiest for it to see.

When later surveys searched more systematically, hot Jupiters turned out to be rare, found around something like one Sun-like star in a hundred. They'd been overrepresented because they were conspicuous, not because they were common.

So is our solar system typical after all? I wouldn't go that far. Plenty of systems found since look nothing like ours either. The honest lesson is narrower: before you ask what's typical, ask what your instrument could have missed.

Transcript: In the early twentieth century, the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski spent several years in the Trobriand Islands, off the coast of New Guinea, and he described an exchange system that seemed, at first, to make no economic sense. It's called the Kula.

Here's how it works. Men sail between islands, sometimes across long stretches of open sea, to exchange two kinds of objects: long necklaces of red shell, and white shell armbands. And the two travel in opposite directions around a great ring of islands. Necklaces move one way, roughly clockwise, and armbands move the other. When you receive a necklace, you'll eventually pass it on to a partner farther along the ring. You don't keep it. Some of these objects are hardly ever worn.

So think about that. People risk dangerous voyages to get things they can't use and won't keep. Why?

Malinowski's answer was that the value lies in holding and passing on, not in owning. A famous necklace carries its history with it, the names of the people who've held it, and having it pass through your hands raises your standing. More importantly, Kula partnerships last for life. A man has fixed partners on other islands, and those relationships give him hosts, allies, and safe passage in places where he'd otherwise be a stranger.

Now, here's the twist that's easy to miss. Alongside the ceremonial exchange, ordinary trade went on: food, pottery, tools, bartered with haggling, the kind of bargaining the Kula itself was supposed to rule out. So the Kula wasn't a replacement for practical trade. It was more like the framework that made practical trade possible, a network of trust stretched across the sea.

The broader lesson, and economic anthropologists still argue about it, is that exchange doesn't have to be about getting things. Sometimes it's about building the relationships that everything else depends on.

Transcript: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, is often called the most successful environmental treaty ever written, and honestly, I think that reputation's earned. Every member of the United Nations eventually ratified it. It phased out chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, the chemicals in old refrigerators and spray cans that drift up into the stratosphere and break down ozone. And measurements now show the ozone layer beginning to recover.

So why am I not just celebrating? Two reasons.

The first is time. A CFC molecule released decades ago can stay in the atmosphere for fifty years or more, some types for around a century. So even though production has basically stopped, the chlorine already up there keeps doing damage. The Antarctic ozone hole still opens every spring, and current projections don't have it fully healing until somewhere around the 2060s. A ban changes what goes into the air. It doesn't instantly change what's already there.

The second reason is more interesting. What replaced CFCs? Over time, largely a family of chemicals called HFCs. They contain no chlorine, so they're harmless to ozone. Problem solved, right? Well, no. Many HFCs turned out to be extremely powerful greenhouse gases, some thousands of times more potent than carbon dioxide, molecule for molecule. The fix for one problem was quietly feeding another.

To its credit, the treaty system responded. In 2016, countries agreed on the Kigali Amendment, which schedules a phase-down of HFCs as well. So the story still ends reasonably well.

But notice what happened. The original choice was judged against a single question: does this harm the ozone layer? HFCs passed that test perfectly. Nobody pressed the broader question until the replacements were already in millions of air conditioners. When you swap out a harmful substance, you have to judge its replacement against every problem, not only the one you're trying to solve.

Transcript: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, is often called the most successful environmental treaty ever written, and honestly, I think that reputation's earned. Every member of the United Nations eventually ratified it. It phased out chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, the chemicals in old refrigerators and spray cans that drift up into the stratosphere and break down ozone. And measurements now show the ozone layer beginning to recover.

So why am I not just celebrating? Two reasons.

The first is time. A CFC molecule released decades ago can stay in the atmosphere for fifty years or more, some types for around a century. So even though production has basically stopped, the chlorine already up there keeps doing damage. The Antarctic ozone hole still opens every spring, and current projections don't have it fully healing until somewhere around the 2060s. A ban changes what goes into the air. It doesn't instantly change what's already there.

The second reason is more interesting. What replaced CFCs? Over time, largely a family of chemicals called HFCs. They contain no chlorine, so they're harmless to ozone. Problem solved, right? Well, no. Many HFCs turned out to be extremely powerful greenhouse gases, some thousands of times more potent than carbon dioxide, molecule for molecule. The fix for one problem was quietly feeding another.

Transcript: Here's a problem that bothered musicians for centuries, and it comes straight out of arithmetic. Take a note and go up by a pure fifth, the interval where the frequencies are in a simple three-to-two ratio. Do that twelve times and you should, in theory, land back on your starting note, just seven octaves higher. You don't. You overshoot, by roughly a quarter of a semitone. Pure fifths and pure octaves can't be made to close the circle.

So any keyboard tuning is a compromise. Somewhere, some intervals have to be bent. Older tunings kept the most common intervals pure and pushed the leftover error into keys composers rarely used. Play in those keys and certain chords sounded so harsh that musicians nicknamed one of the bad intervals the wolf, because it howled.

The modern solution, equal temperament, spreads the error evenly. Every fifth is shaved by the same tiny amount, so every key sounds alike, and you can play in any of them. That's the tuning on nearly every piano today.

You've probably heard that Bach wrote The Well-Tempered Clavier, a set of preludes and fugues in all twenty-four major and minor keys, to show off equal temperament. That's the textbook version. But many scholars now doubt it. Well-tempered isn't the same thing as equally tempered. There were tunings in Bach's day that made every key usable while still leaving them slightly different, so some keys sounded calm and pure and others tenser. If Bach had one of those in mind, his collection wasn't proving that all keys are the same. It was showing that all keys were playable, each with its own character.

We can't be certain which tuning Bach used; he never wrote it down. But the point is worth holding onto: something was lost when every key started to sound the same.

Transcript: During the Second World War, American shipyards built more than two thousand Liberty ships, cargo vessels put together at astonishing speed. Part of that speed came from welding. Instead of riveting steel plates together, as shipbuilders traditionally had, the yards welded them, which was faster and needed less skilled labor.

Then the ships started cracking. Many developed serious fractures, and some broke in two. One welded tanker from the same program split apart while it was tied up at the dock, in calm water. So the obvious suspect was the welding: bad welds, rushed work, done by people who'd only just learned the trade.

And poor welds did play a part. But here's what investigators eventually worked out, and it's the real lesson. Many fractures happened in cold water, in steel that passed the standard tests at room temperature. The researcher Constance Tipper, working at Cambridge, showed that the steel itself behaved differently as it got colder. Above a certain temperature it was ductile: under stress it would stretch and bend before it failed. Below that temperature it turned brittle, and a crack could race through it like a crack through glass, with very little warning.

So why did welding matter? Partly because a riveted hull is made of separate plates, and a crack running through one plate tends to stop at its edge. A welded hull is effectively one continuous piece of steel. Once a crack got going, there was nothing to stop it. Square corners on the hatch openings made things worse by concentrating stress, giving cracks a place to start.

So the failure wasn't one mistake. It was steel that turned brittle in the cold, a building method that let cracks run, and a design that helped them begin. Testing at room temperature had told engineers almost nothing about the conditions the ships actually sailed in.

Transcript: Of all the questions in marine biology, one of the oldest is embarrassingly basic: where do eels come from? Aristotle couldn't find eggs or young in them and suggested eels arose from mud. For centuries afterward nobody had a convincing answer, because the eels living in European rivers never seem to breed there.

The breakthrough came from a Danish biologist, Johannes Schmidt, in the early 1900s, and his method was patient and quite clever. Young eel larvae are small, transparent, leaf-shaped creatures that drift in the open ocean, and they grow as they drift. So Schmidt spent years towing fine nets across the Atlantic and recording the size of the larvae he caught. The farther west and south he went, the smaller they got. The very smallest turned up in the Sargasso Sea, a region of the western Atlantic thousands of kilometers from Europe. Smaller larvae mean more recently hatched larvae, so he concluded that's where the eels spawn.

It's a beautiful piece of reasoning. But notice what kind of reasoning it is. It's an inference from a gradient. In the century since, as far as I know, nobody has seen wild European eels spawning or collected their eggs in the Sargasso. Adult eels heading out to sea have been fitted with tags, and some have been tracked a long way in roughly the right direction, but the final scene has never been witnessed.

Does that mean Schmidt was wrong? I'd be surprised. The larval evidence has held up, and nothing better has come along. But be clear about the kind of confidence we have. It's a detective's confidence when every clue points to one suspect, but nobody actually saw the crime.

And that gap matters in practice, because the European eel is now critically endangered, and it's hard to protect a breeding ground you've never actually observed.

Transcript: Of all the questions in marine biology, one of the oldest is embarrassingly basic: where do eels come from? Aristotle couldn't find eggs or young in them and suggested eels arose from mud. For centuries afterward nobody had a convincing answer, because the eels living in European rivers never seem to breed there.

The breakthrough came from a Danish biologist, Johannes Schmidt, in the early 1900s, and his method was patient and quite clever. Young eel larvae are small, transparent, leaf-shaped creatures that drift in the open ocean, and they grow as they drift. So Schmidt spent years towing fine nets across the Atlantic and recording the size of the larvae he caught. The farther west and south he went, the smaller they got. The very smallest turned up in the Sargasso Sea, a region of the western Atlantic thousands of kilometers from Europe. Smaller larvae mean more recently hatched larvae, so he concluded that's where the eels spawn.

It's a beautiful piece of reasoning. But notice what kind of reasoning it is. It's an inference from a gradient. In the century since, as far as I know, nobody has seen wild European eels spawning or collected their eggs in the Sargasso. Adult eels heading out to sea have been fitted with tags, and some have been tracked a long way in roughly the right direction, but the final scene has never been witnessed.

Does that mean Schmidt was wrong? I'd be surprised. The larval evidence has held up, and nothing better has come along. But be clear about the kind of confidence we have. It's a detective's confidence when every clue points to one suspect, but nobody actually saw the crime.

And that gap matters in practice, because the European eel is now critically endangered, and it's hard to protect a breeding ground you've never actually observed.

Transcript: Here's an experiment that sounds almost too simple. In the late 1990s, an ecologist working in the western United States clipped the leaves of sagebrush plants with scissors, imitating a grazing insect. Wild tobacco plants growing next to the clipped sagebrush then suffered less damage from leaf-eating insects over the season than tobacco growing next to untouched sagebrush. Nothing touched the tobacco. So what happened?

The best explanation is airborne chemistry. Damaged sagebrush releases a burst of volatile compounds, and nearby plants seem to respond by ramping up their own defenses. Later work found that sagebrush responds to cues from other sagebrush, too, and, interestingly, it seems to respond more strongly when the damaged neighbor is a close relative.

Now, the popular version of this is that plants talk to each other, that they warn their neighbors. I'd be careful with that word. Think about it from the damaged plant's point of view. Why would it pay to alert a competitor growing a meter away, one that's fighting it for water and light? Usually it wouldn't. The tobacco plant that picks up the signal benefits, sure, but that looks less like a warning and more like eavesdropping.

So why release the chemicals at all? One idea some researchers favor is that the main audience is the plant itself. In sagebrush, the internal plumbing that carries water and nutrients is divided into sectors, so a chemical message traveling inside the plant may never reach a branch on the far side. Air, though, reaches everything. On that view, the plant is signaling to its own distant branches, and the neighbors are just overhearing.

That doesn't settle it, and the result with relatives still needs explaining. But whenever you hear the word communication, ask who actually benefits.

Transcript: On La Gomera, one of the Canary Islands, there's a way of speaking Spanish without using your voice at all. It's called Silbo Gomero, and it's whistled. The island is cut by deep ravines, and a whistle can carry across a valley, up to a few kilometers in good conditions, where a shout would die out. And it's not a code with a fixed list of messages. Skilled whistlers can say more or less anything they could say in spoken Spanish.

So how do you whistle a language? A whistle has basically one dimension to play with: pitch. Whistlers map the sounds of speech onto changes in pitch. Vowels become different pitch levels, and consonants show up in the way the pitch rises, falls, or breaks off between them. A lot of information gets lost, obviously, and listeners lean heavily on context.

Here's where it gets interesting for the brain. About twenty years ago, researchers scanned experienced Silbo whistlers and found that whistled Spanish activated the same left-hemisphere regions that handle spoken language. In people who didn't know Silbo, those regions didn't respond that way. That was taken as nice evidence that the brain's language areas care about language, not about the kind of sound it arrives in.

But a later study, on a whistled form of Turkish used in a village in northeastern Turkey, complicated the picture. With a listening test that sends different sounds to each ear, researchers found that whistled Turkish drew on both hemispheres far more evenly than spoken Turkish did. Now, the right hemisphere is generally better at handling melody and pitch, and whistling is all pitch.

So which is it? Probably both. The left hemisphere's lead in language looks real, but it isn't absolute. How a language reaches the ear seems to change how the brain divides the work.

Transcript: When a highway gets congested, the obvious fix is to add lanes. More room, less traffic, right? It's intuitive, and it mostly doesn't work, at least not for long.

Economists have looked at this carefully. One well-known American study compared metropolitan areas over a couple of decades and found that the total amount of driving grew roughly in proportion to the amount of new road built. Add ten percent more lane capacity, and you get something close to ten percent more driving. So where do the new drivers come from? Some people who used to take the bus switch to driving. Some who traveled at off-peak hours move back into rush hour. Businesses and new housing locate near the faster road. The space fills up. Planners call this induced demand.

Now, if adding roads creates traffic, does removing roads make traffic disappear? Seoul offers a famous test. In the early 2000s, the city tore down an elevated highway that ran over the Cheonggyecheon stream, which had been paved over decades earlier, and restored the stream as a public park. Plenty of people predicted gridlock. It didn't happen. Traffic in the surrounding area didn't get dramatically worse, and some drivers simply stopped making those trips by car.

But be careful about the lesson. Seoul didn't just remove a road. Around the same time, the city reorganized its whole bus system, with dedicated bus lanes and a new fare system, and it already had an extensive subway. The drivers who vanished had somewhere to go. Take away a highway in a city where the car is the only realistic option, and you may simply push the traffic onto neighboring streets.

So traffic responds to road space in both directions. It just doesn't respond in a vacuum.

Economists have looked at this carefully. One well-known American study compared metropolitan areas over a couple of decades and found that the total amount of driving grew roughly in proportion to the amount of new road built. Add ten percent more lane capacity, and you get something close to ten percent more driving. So where do the new drivers come from? Some people who used to take the bus switch to driving. Some who traveled at off-peak hours move back into rush hour. Businesses and new housing locate near the faster road. The space fills up. Planners call this induced demand.

Now, if adding roads creates traffic, does removing roads make traffic disappear? Seoul offers a famous test. In the early 2000s, the city tore down an elevated highway that ran over the Cheonggyecheon stream, which had been paved over decades earlier, and restored the stream as a public park. Plenty of people predicted gridlock. It didn't happen. Traffic in the surrounding area didn't get dramatically worse, and some drivers simply stopped making those trips by car.

But be careful about the lesson. Seoul didn't just remove a road. Around the same time, the city reorganized its whole bus system, with dedicated bus lanes and a new fare system, and it already had an extensive subway. The drivers who vanished had somewhere to go. Take away a highway in a city where the car is the only realistic option, and you may simply push the traffic onto neighboring streets.

So traffic responds to road space in both directions. It just doesn't respond in a vacuum.

Transcript: You've probably heard of tulip mania. In the Dutch Republic in the 1630s, the story goes, people went mad for tulip bulbs. Single bulbs sold for the price of a house, ordinary people mortgaged everything, and when prices collapsed in early 1637, the country was ruined. Some versions add merchants throwing themselves into canals. It's the classic tale of a bubble, and much of it was popularized two centuries later, in 1841, by a Scottish writer named Charles Mackay.

The trouble is, when historians went back to the archives, the ruin is hard to find. One historian, Anne Goldgar, worked through contracts, court records, and notaries' papers from the period, and she found very few bankruptcies that could be tied to tulips. The trade seems to have been concentrated among fairly well-off merchants and craftsmen, not the poor. And the Dutch economy appears to have kept growing through the late 1630s. So where did the stories of mass ruin come from? Largely from moralizing pamphlets printed right after the crash, which used tulips to preach against greed. Mackay leaned on material like that.

Now, I don't want to swing too far the other way. Prices really did spike, and they really did collapse. That part is well documented. Some rare varieties changed hands for astonishing sums. And a lot of the trading in the final months was in contracts for bulbs still in the ground, so when buyers refused to pay, there were real disputes, and some of them dragged on for a while.

What the evidence undermines is the idea that the crash was an economic disaster. A price bubble and a financial catastrophe aren't the same thing. One can happen without the other, and here, it seems, it mostly did.

Transcript: For most of the twentieth century, the textbook rule was that you're born with all the neurons you'll ever have. Then, starting in the 1960s and especially in the 1990s, studies in rats and mice showed that new neurons keep being born in adult brains, in one region in particular: the hippocampus, which is crucial for memory. The obvious next question is whether the same is true for us. And here, the field is still arguing.

Some of the evidence is clever. One team took advantage of the nuclear weapons tests of the 1950s and 60s, which raised the level of carbon-14 in the atmosphere. That carbon ended up in the DNA of cells born during those years, so by measuring it in brains donated after death, researchers could estimate when the neurons had been born. Their estimate was that adults add something like seven hundred new neurons a day to the hippocampus.

But in 2018, one group looked directly at hippocampal tissue, staining for markers that young neurons carry, and found essentially none in adults. In babies, yes. In young teenagers, a few. In adults, almost nothing. Another lab published the opposite result that same year.

How can two careful labs disagree that much? One possibility is the tissue itself. Human brain samples are collected hours after death and preserved in different ways, and some of the markers for young neurons seem to fade quickly if the tissue isn't preserved right away. A follow-up study that controlled preservation tightly did find young neurons, even in people in their late eighties.

So here's where I land. The case for adult neurogenesis in humans looks stronger now than it did in 2018, but the debate isn't over, and what's being argued about is partly the methods, not just the brain.

Transcript: For most of the history of paleontology, the colors in dinosaur reconstructions were pure guesswork. Artists borrowed from lizards or birds and made something up. Then, around 2010, that changed, at least for a few species.

The key was a tiny structure called a melanosome. It's a capsule inside cells that holds melanin, the pigment behind black, gray, brown, and some reddish-brown colors in modern birds and mammals. Under powerful microscopes, fossil feathers turned out to contain tiny bodies with the shapes of melanosomes. And the shape matters. In living birds, long, thin, sausage-shaped melanosomes tend to go with black and gray, while rounder ones tend to go with reddish-brown. So by measuring fossil melanosomes, researchers proposed that a small feathered dinosaur from China, Sinosauropteryx, had a tail banded in reddish-brown and white.

Now, here's an irony. Those same tiny bodies had been spotted in fossils decades earlier, and researchers had interpreted them as fossilized bacteria. That wasn't unreasonable, since bacteria are about the same size and shape. A few scientists still argue that at least some of these structures are microbes.
